notes: One record per claim we rely on, in our words. Each claim is checked against the paper note in research/papers/ (and through it, the paper). confidence here = confidence in the claim as stated (DATA_MODEL.md §6).

evidence.claim: Neandertals share more derived variants with present-day people outside sub-Saharan Africa than with sub-Saharan Africans, best explained by gene flow from Neandertals into the ancestors of non-Africans before Eurasian populations diverged.
A finger bone from Denisova Cave yielded the genome of an archaic group related to Neandertals, named Denisovans.
Denisovan-related ancestry was first estimated at 4–6% of the genomes of present-day Melanesians.
evidence.location: Abstract; section on Denisovan gene flow into Melanesians
evidence.note: First estimate; later work refines Denisovan proportions.

evidence.claim: Neandertal-derived DNA in people outside Africa was estimated at 1.5–2.1%.
evidence.location: Gene-flow section; SI 14; Extended Data Table 1

evidence.claim: The Neandertal ancestry in non-Africans is closer to the Mezmaiskaya (Caucasus) Neandertal than to the Altai Neandertal.
Gene flow from Neandertals into Denisovans contributed at least about 0.5% of the Denisovan genome.
The Vindija and Mezmaiskaya Neandertals are closer than the Altai Neandertal to the Neandertals who contributed DNA to present-day non-Africans.
Revised estimate: non-Africans outside Oceania carry 1.8–2.6% Neandertal DNA (East Asians 2.3–2.6%, western Eurasians 1.8–2.4%).
Linkage disequilibrium in present-day Europeans dates the last Neandertal gene flow to 37,000–86,000 years ago, most likely 47,000–65,000 years ago.
Ust'-Ishim (~45,000 years old, western Siberia) belonged to a population that lived before or around the separation of western and eastern Eurasians.
Ust'-Ishim's Neandertal segments are longer than in present-day people, placing the Neandertal gene flow about 7,000–13,000 years before he lived.
Site-frequency-spectrum modelling places a primary Neandertal admixture of about 2.3% (95% CI 1.1–3.5%) in the ancestors of all non-Africans at about 60,000 years ago (95% CI 55–84 ka).
Aboriginal Australians and Papuans carry more Denisovan-derived haplotypes than other non-Africans.
evidence.location: Archaic admixture section; Extended Data Fig. 3

evidence.claim: Most Neandertal ancestry in modern humans traces to a single extended period of gene flow 50,500–43,500 years ago, shared by most non-Africans.

Individuals from Ranis (Germany) and Zlatý kůň (Czechia), about 45,000 years old, belong to one small, closely related population that is the earliest split from the out-of-Africa population sampled so far and shows no continuity with later Europeans.
The Neandertal ancestry of the Zlatý kůň/Ranis population comes from the admixture shared by all non-Africans, dated to 45,000–49,000 years ago.

Three individuals from Bacho Kiro Cave (Bulgaria), dated ~45,900–42,600 years ago and associated with an Initial Upper Palaeolithic assemblage, are more closely related to later East Asians and Native Americans than to later western Eurasians, and each had a Neandertal ancestor a few generations back.
Oase 1 (Romania, ~37,000–42,000 years old) has about 6–9% Neandertal DNA, implying a Neandertal ancestor 4–6 generations back, and shows no special relationship to later Europeans.

Denisovan-introgressed segments in present-day Chinese and Japanese populations fall into two components with different affinity to the Altai Denisovan, indicating at least two Denisovan-related sources.
evidence.location: Section 'Two waves of Denisovan ancestry'; Fig. 4; Table 2

evidence.claim: Ayta Magbukon (Philippines) carry about 30–40% more Denisovan ancestry than Australians and Papuans, consistent with a separate Denisovan admixture event.
Neandertal ancestry in European individuals fell from 3–6% in the earliest to about 2% over 45,000–7,000 years ago.

From about 37,000 years ago (Kostenki 14) to about 14,000 years ago, all sampled Europeans descend from one founder population that is part of present-day European ancestry; earlier individuals such as Oase 1 did not contribute substantially.

Genetically defined clusters, named after type sites: Věstonice (Gravettian-associated), Mal'ta, El Mirón (Magdalenian-associated, with affinity to GoyetQ116-1) and Villabruna (from ~14,000 years ago).
From about 14,000 years ago a component related to present-day Near Easterners appears in Europe with the Villabruna cluster.

Hunter-gatherer clusters before and after the LGM: Fournol (Gravettian-associated, western Europe, related to Aurignacian-associated Goyet Q116-1), Věstonice (Gravettian-associated, central and southern Europe), GoyetQ2 (Magdalenian-associated), Villabruna (Epigravettian-associated), Oberkassel (equated with WHG), and Sidelkino (renamed EHG).
Gravettian-associated individuals form two genetically distinct clusters (Fournol in the west, Věstonice in central and southern Europe): one archaeological culture, two genetic profiles.
Fournol-related ancestry persisted through the LGM in southwestern Europe in Solutrean- and then Magdalenian-associated individuals.
From at least 14,000 years ago, Villabruna/Oberkassel-related ancestry spread from the south across Europe, largely replacing Magdalenian-associated (GoyetQ2) ancestry.
Magdalenian-associated individuals are modelled as mixtures of Fournol- and Villabruna-related ancestry; El Mirón carries about 43% Villabruna-related ancestry, others 19–29%.

From about 8,000 years ago, Sidelkino (EHG)-related ancestry appears at about 10% in central European hunter-gatherers, and Oberkassel-related ancestry reaches the upper Volga by at least 7,500 years ago.
Gravettian-associated individuals from Goyet (Belgium) are genetically intermediate between the Věstonice and Fournol clusters, contrary to their earlier assignment by Fu et al. 2016.
Eastern hunter-gatherer (EHG/Sidelkino) ancestry shows affinity to both Villabruna-related and Ancient North Eurasian ancestry.

Most present-day Europeans can be modelled with ancestry from three deeply differentiated sources: West European Hunter-Gatherers (WHG), Ancient North Eurasians (ANE) and Early European Farmers (EEF).
Early European Farmers are modelled with about 44% ancestry from a 'Basal Eurasian' lineage that split before other non-African lineages diversified.
evidence.note: Basal Eurasian is a modelled lineage without sampled individuals.

evidence.claim: Caucasus hunter-gatherers (Satsurblia ~13,300 years ago, Kotias Klde ~9,700 years ago, western Georgia) form a distinct ancient clade.
Model-based split times: CHG from WHG about 45,000 years ago, and from the ancestors of Neolithic farmers about 25,000 years ago.
CHG-related ancestry contributed significantly to Yamnaya-associated steppe herders.

MA-1 (Mal'ta, south-central Siberia, ~24,000 years ago) is basal to present-day western Eurasians and related to Native Americans, without close affinity to East Asians; Afontova Gora 2 (~17,000 years ago) shows similar ancestry.
An estimated 14–38% of Native American ancestry may derive from gene flow from a population related to MA-1, after divergence from East Asian ancestors and before Native American diversification.

Northeastern Siberia saw an initial Palaeolithic 'Ancient North Siberian' population (Yana, ~31,000 years ago) distantly related to early West Eurasian hunter-gatherers, then East Asian-related people who gave rise to Native Americans and 'Ancient Paleosiberians', then Holocene 'Neosiberians'; each expansion nearly replaced earlier inhabitants.

Seven ~15,000-year-old Iberomaurusian-associated individuals from Taforalt (Morocco) show affinity with Natufians, no gene flow from Palaeolithic Europeans, and about one-third sub-Saharan African-related ancestry.

Tianyuan (~40,000 years old, China) is more related to Asians than to Europeans but shares extra alleles with Goyet Q116-1 (~35,000 years old, Belgium), so early European and Asian populations did not separate in one clean split.
The earliest sampled Near Eastern populations derived about half their ancestry from a 'Basal Eurasian' lineage with little or no Neandertal ancestry.
The first farmers of the southern Levant and of the Zagros were strongly differentiated, each descending largely from local hunter-gatherers.
By the Bronze Age, Levant-, Zagros- and Anatolia-related farmer ancestries had mixed, reducing genetic differentiation across the Near East.
Farmer ancestry related to Anatolian farmers spread west into Europe.
East African ancestry is better modelled by Levantine early farmers than by Anatolian or European farmers: Levant-related farmer ancestry contributed to East Africa.
Ancestry related to Iranian farmers spread north into the Eurasian steppe.
People related to both early Iranian farmers and steppe pastoralists spread east into South Asia.
evidence.note: The Iranian-farmer part is contested by Shinde 2019 and Narasimhan 2019.

evidence.claim: Early Neolithic people of the Zagros were neither ancestral to the first European farmers nor significant contributors to present-day Europeans; multiple differentiated hunter-gatherer populations adopted farming in southwest Asia.
Model-based separation of Zagros and Anatolian early farmers' ancestors: about 46,000–77,000 years ago.

Central Anatolian early farmers show about 80–90% genetic continuity with a ~15,000-year-old local hunter-gatherer (Pınarbaşı), with additional Iranian/Caucasus-related and later Levant-related ancestry.
Late Chalcolithic individuals from Peqi'in Cave (Israel, 4500–3900 BCE) are modelled as about 57% Levant Neolithic-related, 17% Iran Chalcolithic-related and 26% Anatolia Neolithic-related.
Farming reached southeastern Europe in the mid-7th millennium BCE with migrants of Anatolian-related ancestry.
European hunter-gatherers formed a west–east cline of ancestry.
The first farmers of northern and western Europe passed through southeastern Europe with limited hunter-gatherer admixture; some groups that remained there mixed extensively.
Hunter-gatherer ancestry in early European farmers varied by region and generally increased over time through local admixture.
Hunter-gatherer ancestry estimates: LBK about 4–5% (admixture dated 5545 ± 65 BCE); German Middle Neolithic about 17%; Iberian Middle Neolithic about 23%; Iberian Chalcolithic about 27%.

Farming came to Britain with continental farmers whose ancestry was mostly Anatolian-farmer-related (about 74% on average in the authors' model), with small hunter-gatherer contributions and no later hunter-gatherer resurgence.
British Neolithic individuals show affinities with Iberian Neolithic individuals, suggesting descent mainly from farmers who followed the Mediterranean route.
Continental farmers are modelled as arriving in Britain by 3975–3722 cal BCE (95%).

8,000–7,000 years ago, early farmers in Germany, Hungary and Spain were closely related to each other and distinct from local hunter-gatherers, while Russia was inhabited by hunter-gatherers (EHG) with high affinity to the 24,000-year-old Mal'ta individual.
Middle Neolithic populations of Germany and Spain carry about 18–34% more WHG-related ancestry than Early Neolithic populations.
Yamnaya-associated steppe herders descended from eastern European hunter-gatherers and from a population of Near Eastern ancestry.
Corded Ware-associated individuals from Germany derive about 75% of their ancestry from a Yamnaya-related source; modelled against Middle Neolithic populations, the turnover is 48–80%.
Steppe-related ancestry persisted in all sampled central Europeans to at least 3,000 years ago; Bell Beaker- and Únětice-associated groups carry less of it than Corded Ware-associated individuals.
Iberian and central European Beaker-associated individuals had limited genetic affinity, so the Beaker complex spread between these regions mainly through cultural transmission.
Steppe-related ancestry is present in most Beaker-associated individuals outside Iberia, but in only 8 of 32 Iberian Beaker-associated individuals.
In Britain, the arrival of the Beaker complex brought high steppe-related ancestry and was associated with replacement of about 90% of the gene pool within a few hundred years.
Iberian hunter-gatherers showed strong substructure between the northwest and southeast before farming.
By about 2000 BCE, about 40% of Iberia's ancestry and nearly 100% of its Y chromosomes derive from people with steppe-related ancestry: a strongly male-biased process.
A genetic boundary from the Black Sea to the Baltic separated differentiated hunter-gatherers; farming brought large ancestry shifts west of it and none of substance east of it in the same period.
Yamnaya-related ancestry spread across western Eurasia from about 5,000 years ago, reaching most of Europe within about 1,000 years.
Middle Don hunter-gatherers contributed ancestry to Yamnaya-associated groups, which later admixed with Globular Amphora-associated people before expanding into Europe.
Gene flow carried Caucasus- and Anatolian/Levantine-related ancestry north to the steppe; Yamnaya-associated people later spread into the Balkans and across the Caucasus into Armenia.
Bronze Age Anatolia was shaped by gene flow within West Asia, with negligible impact from Yamnaya-related migrations.

The Yamnaya archaeological complex appeared about 3300 BCE north of the Black and Caspian Seas and by 3000 BCE extended from Hungary to Kazakhstan; its individuals are genetically very similar across this range.

Eneolithic people north of the Caucasus form three clines: Caucasus–Lower Volga (CLV, rich in CHG-related ancestry), Volga (CLV mixed with EHG, e.g. Khvalynsk), and Dnipro (CLV mixed with Ukraine Neolithic hunter-gatherers, e.g. Serednii Stih).
Yamnaya ancestors formed about 4000 BCE from Serednii Stih-related groups and grew rapidly after 3750–3350 BCE; CLV-related people contributed about four-fifths of Yamnaya ancestry.
Don Yamnaya are modelled as 79.4 ± 1.1% 'Core Yamnaya' and 20.6 ± 1.1% Ukraine Neolithic hunter-gatherer-related ancestry (qpAdm).
Usatove-associated people formed as CLV-related migrants mixed in roughly equal parts with Trypillia-associated farmers.
A genetically Yamnaya-like individual from Mykhailivka (3635–3383 BCE) bridges Serednii Stih and Yamnaya.
Groups of the Caucasus mountains were genetically separated from contemporaneous steppe groups; Yamnaya and later steppe pastoralists carry farmer-related ancestry from different contact zones.
Botai-associated people, linked to the earliest horse husbandry, derive from hunter-gatherers deeply diverged from the Yamnaya.
No steppe-related ancestry was found in Bronze Age Anatolia, and Early Bronze Age Yamnaya-related migrations had limited direct genetic impact in Asia compared with Europe.

Between 1000 and 875 BCE, EEF-related ancestry increased in southern Britain through migrants genetically most similar to ancient individuals from France, who contributed about half the ancestry of Iron Age people of England and Wales.
The main source of ancestry in South Asians is a prehistoric gradient between people related to early Iranian hunter-gatherers and people related to South/Southeast Asian hunter-gatherers (AASI).
Eleven outlier individuals at Gonur and Shahr-i-Sokhta form an 'Indus Periphery Cline'; equating it with the Indus Valley Civilization population is a hypothesis with circumstantial support.

After the IVC's decline, Indus Periphery-related people mixed with south-eastern groups to form Ancestral South Indians (ASI), and with steppe-pastoralist-descended people arriving via Central Asia after ~4000 years ago to form Ancestral North Indians (ANI).
AASI ('Ancestral Ancient South Asians') is modelled as an Asian lineage that split around the time East Asian, Andamanese and Australian ancestors separated.
Steppe-related ancestry in South Asia has the same profile as that of Bronze Age eastern Europe.

A genome from an IVC context (Rakhigarhi) fits as a mixture of ancient-Iranian-related (largest) and Southeast Asian hunter-gatherer-related ancestry, matching the Indus Periphery outliers, with little or no steppe-related ancestry.

The Iranian-related ancestry in the IVC individual derives from a lineage that split before the ancestors of early Iranian farmers, herders and hunter-gatherers separated, contradicting a large-scale eastward spread of western Iranian farmers.
Jōmon-associated hunter-gatherers, Amur Basin hunter-gatherers, and Neolithic/Iron Age Taiwan and Tibetan-plateau people share a deeply splitting lineage.
evidence.note: The authors' interpretation as a Late Pleistocene coastal migration is not displayed as a route.

evidence.claim: Yellow River farmer-related ancestry (around 3000 BCE) contributed up to about 84% to some Tibetan groups and about 59–84% to Han Chinese.

Individuals from Taiwan (~1300 BCE–800 CE) derive about 75% of their ancestry from a southern lineage (likely Yangtze-farmer-related) and about 25% from a northern lineage related to but distinct from Yellow River farmers.
Yamnaya-related steppe ancestry reached western Mongolia after about 3000 BCE.

Amur River populations were genetically stable from 7500 to 1700 BP, while Yellow River and West Liao River profiles changed; Yellow River populations grew increasingly similar to present-day southern Chinese and Southeast Asians over time.
In the West Liao River region, Late Neolithic farming intensification coincides with increased Yellow River affinity, and Bronze Age pastoralism with increased Amur affinity.
Northern East Asian ancestry spread across southern East Asia after the Neolithic; Neolithic southern East Asian and Taiwan Strait individuals show Austronesian-related connections.

Early farmers at Man Bac (Vietnam) mix East Asian (southern-Chinese-agriculturalist-related) and deeply diverged eastern Eurasian hunter-gatherer ancestry; by the Bronze Age, sites in Vietnam and Myanmar show further influxes.
Both Hòabìnhian hunter-gatherer-related and East Asian farmer-related ancestry contributed to Southeast Asian diversity.
Japanese archipelago: Jōmon-related ancestry, then Northeast Asian-related ancestry in the Yayoi period, then East Asian-related ancestry in the Kofun period.
A ~2,500-year-old Jōmon-context individual (IK002) forms a lineage basal to the East and Northeast Asian genomes examined.
A pastoralist expansion reached Mongolia around 3000 BCE; by the Late Bronze Age three genetically structured groups all practised dairy pastoralism regardless of ancestry.
Xiongnu-period individuals formed from mixture of earlier Mongolian and surrounding populations; Mongol-period individuals show much higher eastern Eurasian ancestry.
Anzick-1, an infant buried with Clovis tools in Montana (~12,700–12,550 cal BP), is more closely related to all Indigenous American populations than to any other group.
The ANE (Mal'ta)-related gene flow into Native American ancestors is shared by Anzick-1, so it happened before about 12,600 years ago.
The ancestors of all present-day Native Americans entered the Americas from Siberia as a single migration wave no earlier than 23,000 years ago, after at most ~8,000 years of isolation in Beringia.
Native Americans diversified into two basal branches around 13,000 years ago.

Later gene flow led some Native Americans to share ancestry with present-day East Asians and, more distantly, with Australo-Melanesians; putative 'Paleoamerican' relict groups are not directly related to Australo-Melanesians.
USR1 (Upward Sun River, Alaska, ~11,500 years ago) is basal to all other Native Americans and represents a distinct Ancient Beringian population.

Demographic model: split from East Asians ~36 ± 1.5 ka with gene flow until ~25 ka; ANE-related gene flow 25–20 ka; Ancient Beringians branched 22–18.1 ka; northern and southern Native American branches diverged 17.5–14.6 ka.
Some Amazonian groups carry ancestry from a founding source ('Population Y') with extra affinity to Australasians, not seen in Anzick-1 or North and Central Americans.
evidence.note: Signal from present-day genomes; source population unsampled.

evidence.claim: Rapid early dispersal and diversification within the Americas, including one migration with an Australasian-related signal and a later Mesoamerican-related expansion.
Central and South Americans radiated rapidly from one of the two early Native American branches.
Two streams of North–South gene flow: one reaching the Central Andes by about 4,200 years ago, and one linking Anzick-1 to the oldest individuals from Chile, Brazil and Belize.
Later South Americans derive from lineages without specific Clovis affinity: a population replacement beginning at least 9,000 years ago, followed by substantial regional continuity.

Present-day Andean genetic structure began to form by about 5,800 years ago; neighbouring Andean groups show minimal admixture 2,000–500 years ago, with mixed-ancestry communities in the Tiwanaku and Inca heartlands.
Archaic Age Caribbean people derive from a deeply divergent population closest to Central and northern South Americans.

Archaic Caribbean lineages were more than 98% replaced by a homogeneous ceramic-using population related to Arawak speakers of northeastern South America, which reached the Greater Antilles at least 1,700 years ago.
Changes in pottery style within the Ceramic Age were not driven by migration of genetically distinct groups.
Human footprints at White Sands (New Mexico) are bracketed by seed layers with calibrated radiocarbon ages of about 23,000–21,000 years ago.
evidence.note: Archaeological evidence; dating debated in later literature not yet reviewed here.

evidence.claim: Lapita-associated individuals from Vanuatu (~3,100–2,700 years ago) and Tonga (~2,700–2,300 years ago) had little or no Papuan-related ancestry.
Present-day South Pacific populations carry at least 25% Papuan-related ancestry, which must have spread after first settlement.
The first Remote Oceanians descend directly from the population that spread from Taiwan via the Philippines to western Melanesia from about 5,000 years ago, with minimal admixture along the way.
People of almost entirely Papuan-related ancestry reached Vanuatu by about 2,300 years ago; Papuan-related ancestry was later diluted but remains at least 80–90% on most islands.
The Papuan-related ancestry in Vanuatu derives from the Bismarck Archipelago.

A Papuan-related expansion into Remote Oceania began about 2,500 years ago and led to near-complete replacement of Lapita-related ancestry in Vanuatu through repeated migrations and sex-biased admixture, while Austronesian languages persisted.

Present-day genomes suggest a serial-founder settlement of Polynesia from Samoa through Rarotonga to the Society Islands (~11th century), Austral and Tuāmotu (~12th century), and Marquesas, Raivavae and Rapa Nui (~1200 CE).

San-related ancestry was once more widespread: about two-thirds of the ancestry of Malawi hunter-gatherers (~8,100–2,500 years ago) and about one-third of Tanzanian hunter-gatherers (~1,400 years ago).
The spread of farmers from western Africa involved complete replacement of local hunter-gatherers in some regions.

A ~3,100-year-old pastoralist from Luxmanda (Tanzania) is modelled with 38 ± 1% ancestry related to Levantine pre-pottery farmers (Iran- or Anatolia-related sources excluded); the authors note this could reflect migration from the Levant or a shared earlier ancestral population.

Children buried at Shum Laka (Cameroon) ~8,000 and ~3,000 years ago have ancestry most similar to west-central African hunter-gatherers; present-day Bantu speakers do not descend substantially from this population.
Eastern and south-central African forager ancestry is a geographically structured mixture of three highly divergent sources, probably formed 80,000–20,000 years ago and stable afterwards.

East African pastoralist groups formed through admixture between northeastern-African-related peoples and eastern African foragers, with further northeastern- and western-African-related admixture by the Iron Age.
Makers of distinct Pastoral Neolithic artefact traditions were not genetically differentiated.
Kenyan pastoralist individuals carry variable Dinka-related and eastern-forager-related ancestry (e.g. 33 ± 11% Dinka-related at Hyrax Hill, ~2,300 years ago).
Genetic diversity among Bantu-speaking populations declines with distance from western Africa, supporting a serial-founder expansion, with significant gene flow from local groups.
~2,000-year-old Stone Age individuals from KwaZulu-Natal resemble present-day southern San; Iron Age individuals (300–500 years old) resemble present-day Bantu-language speakers.

Many medieval Swahili coast individuals derive more than half their DNA from African ancestors (mainly female-line) and much of the rest from Asian ancestors, 80–90% of whose DNA traces to Persian-related men; mixing began by about 1000 CE.

After a 2016 erratum, Mota (Ethiopia, ~4,500 years old) is retained as a high-coverage eastern African genome predating Eurasian-related admixture in eastern Africa; the original claim of Eurasian ancestry in Yoruba and Mbuti was withdrawn.
